# showrunner

> A multi-agent orchestrator for Claude Code. If you are an AI agent working in a repo that has a
> `.showrunner/` directory, this file tells you how to operate it. Everything below is a command you
> run, not a rule you remember.

showrunner decomposes work into a dependency graph, sends a party of agents into separate git
worktrees in parallel, enforces the party-wide rules no single agent can see (above all: a
cross-process lock over shared single-consumer resources), and keeps the campaign coherent across
sessions. It is the horizontal counterpart to **game_loop**'s vertical, single-session survival rails.
Both game_loop and **br** are optional and neither knows showrunner exists.

**Crawler** is the only term you need: one Claude Code session, in its own worktree, with its own
scratch dir and its own brief, working one leaf. The naming is themed and the docs lean on it; the
definition is the whole of what it means here.

The design rule everything follows from, inherited from the layer below: **enforcement lives in tools
and artifacts, never in instructions.** Test any guard by asking — *if I ignored every instruction,
would it still hold?* And the rule showrunner adds, because its guards are cross-process: **a degraded
guard must fail loud, never quiet.** A mutex that is silently a no-op is worse than no mutex, because
nobody inside a single Crawler can observe the collision.

`showrunner` is **not a global command** — it is the project-local binary
`./.showrunner/bin/showrunner`. Call it by that path. Python 3 standard library only; nothing to
install.

## First thing, every session

```
./.showrunner/bin/showrunner doctor     # refuses a config that would degrade silently
./.showrunner/bin/showrunner status     # ready / claimed / parked / locks / stale claims
```

`doctor` exits non-zero on anything that would degrade **silently**: no config at all (every check
below it then runs against defaults nobody chose), a lock root that is not one absolute shared
path, a worktree root outside the repo, a configured chat path that does not resolve, or a missing
`.showrunner/bin/showrunner` — the binary every Crawler brief names. Fix the config; do not route
around it.

It also **warns** about the one thing a human has to do by hand: arming the harness's idle
watchdog. Point it at `.showrunner/hooks/waiting-probe.sh`, **not** at `showrunner waiting`
directly — the verb answers three exit codes (0 waiting, 1 not waiting, 3 a Crawler is BLOCKED)
and a two-state watchdog reads that third one as "the probe is broken". The probe maps them, and
never answers "waiting" from inside a worktree, where a Crawler would otherwise silence its own
watchdog with a sibling's liveness.

You cannot do this for the operator — a probe an agent can set is a watchdog an agent can switch
off — so if you are running unattended, say that it is unarmed rather than proceeding quietly.

## If you are the ORCHESTRATOR

```
showrunner ready                     # unblocked AND unclaimed leaves — the only discovery entrypoint
showrunner plan                      # group them into waves whose estimated file sets do not overlap
showrunner route                     # which lane each leaf takes, and the rule that decided
showrunner spawn <leaf> --actor <name> [--base <ref>] [--finding "<already checked>"]
                                     # prints the base it cuts from, and REFUSES to be quiet when
                                     # a graph dependency's branch is not in it
                                     # prepares the room: worktree, branch, scratch, brief, lock, claim
showrunner spawn <leaf> --launch     # ...and STARTS a real Claude Code session in it, with its own
                                     # hooks, on the model its lane declares. --dry-run to see the
                                     # command and start nothing. Without --launch, spawn prepares
                                     # and stops, and you start the agent yourself.
showrunner integrate                 # serial merge, checks re-run on each MERGED result

# A chat room is NOT optional under --launch. A Crawler refused at its turn-end stays alive
# and inert, and a message is the only thing that restarts it. Nothing is vendored:
# git clone https://github.com/SupposedlySam/llm_chat.git ../llm_chat
# then dispatch.chat = {enabled, cli, installer}. Without it, use spawn WITHOUT --launch and
# drive the Crawlers yourself. Machine-specific paths go in .showrunner/config.local.json.
showrunner reap                      # dry run; --apply to reclaim dead Crawlers' claims and locks,
                                     # close rooms they left open, and SIGTERM processes that
                                     # outlived their leaf. `close` already closed the room and
                                     # marked the Crawler finished; this catches what died badly.
showrunner reconcile                 # on resume: merged / abandoned / live / BLOCKED — ask FIRST
showrunner amend <leaf> --premise .. # correct a CLOSED leaf's premise by SUPERSEDING it: the
                                     # original verdict stays readable, because a record that can
                                     # be edited is one nobody can cite later
```

## Watching a campaign live

```
showrunner snapshot                  # the whole world, ONE call, one instant
showrunner watch --follow            # ...then the deltas. One JSON object per line.
showrunner watch --since <cursor>    # resume: only what came after
```

**Snapshot first, then watch.** An event saying `leaf.closed` is not a picture, it is a delta
against one — so a viewer needs the state before the stream means anything. `snapshot` carries
ready leaves, in-progress leaves, every Crawler with its verdict, every resource with its
holder, and the waiting verdict. Assembling that from `status` + `reconcile` + `waiting` + `plan`
costs four round trips and hands you a composite of instants that never co-existed.

The two join on `cursor`. `snapshot`'s cursor names the last event it could have seen, so
`watch --since <that>` gives you exactly what is not already reflected — no overlap to
de-duplicate and no gap to guess at. It is **not** a transaction: nothing freezes the graph, so
parts can still disagree by milliseconds. What it removes is the four-call window.

**How fresh is the crawler report, and will anything look again?** `reconcile` opens with
`checked`, `last re-check` and `next re-check`, and `snapshot` carries the same as `follow_up`.
A report says what is true at the instant it runs, and without these a reading taken thirty
seconds ago is indistinguishable from one taken yesterday — and nothing tells you whether
walking away from a fan-out is safe.

Both facts are the **harness's** idle watchdog's, and both are asked rather than assumed. So
`next re-check` names a **trigger, not a time**: the watchdog fires on idle and its porcelain
answer publishes no interval, so a clock time here would be a number showrunner invented about
an event it does not schedule. When no probe is armed — the default — it says `NONE SCHEDULED`
and why, because a report with no follow-up must not look like one with a follow-up.

`status` and `reconcile` answer **what is true now**. `watch` answers **what just happened** — a
leaf claimed, a lock refused, a Crawler blocked, an integrate rewound. Ask these rather than
reading `.showrunner/events.jsonl`: the file's name and layout are showrunner's business, and a
consumer that reaches past the verb breaks the next time either changes.

The event kinds, and what each is for:

| kind | why a view needs it |
|---|---|
| `leaf.added` · `claimed` · `released` · `parked` · `unparked` · `closed` | the work moving |
| `crawler.spawned` · `crawler.state` | a Crawler's lifecycle, every transition through one chokepoint |
| `crawler.blocked` · `crawler.unblocked` | alive and doing nothing. The state that most needs a human, and the only one every other signal reads as healthy |
| `lock.acquired` · `released` · **`refused`** · **`reclaimed`** | the serialization point no single Crawler can see. A refusal is how you draw a QUEUE; without it a contended resource and an idle one are the same picture. `reclaimed` is a reaper taking a resource off a dead holder — not the holder letting go |
| `integrate.*` | the riskiest verb, one kind per outcome: integrated, conflict, would-merge, checks-failed-on-merged-result, harness-drifted |

`crawler.blocked` is journalled on the **transition**, not on the state — `reconcile` recomputes
it every call, so a poller would otherwise get one identical line per poll.

Frames carry their own type. `ready` marks the end of the replay, so attaching to a running
campaign is never a blank screen. `heartbeat` proves the stream is alive — the journal is sparse
by design and an orchestrator can integrate for twenty minutes without writing one event, so
silence is normal and a stream that has DIED looks the same. `bye` marks a clean end; a stream
that simply stops did not end, it broke.

**The cursor names its instance, and `--since` refuses one from a different showrunner.** A seq
counts within one journal. Several showrunners in several repos is the ordinary case, so a bare
integer crossing that boundary is a confident answer about a different campaign — both sides
integers, the comparison succeeding, nothing able to notice.

**If you are relaying these somewhere, the cursor is the CONSUMER's.** `watch` keeps no durable
position; you supply yours. Never record a cursor as proof of delivery before whatever you are
feeding has actually taken the frames — that turns at-least-once into at-most-once, silently.

## One session per worktree

```
showrunner lease status [<tree>]     # which trees are held, by whom, and on what evidence
showrunner worktree enter            # SessionStart: take this tree's lease, or report who holds it
showrunner worktree fork --from <t>  # your own tree, off the same base commit as a held one
showrunner worktree guard            # PreToolUse: DENY a write into a tree another live session holds
showrunner worktree register         # put ALL FOUR hooks in .claude/settings.json (idempotent):
                                     # the worktree guard and the dispatch guard on PreToolUse,
                                     # the inert-Crawler gate on Stop, and the seat announcement
                                     # on SessionStart AND PostCompact
showrunner whoami                    # what this session IS — a seat DERIVED from where it stands
showrunner whoami --porcelain        # the SAME resolution as JSON, for a guard to consume
showrunner role claim <role>         # take an open seat (a role declaring acquire=claim)
showrunner role release <role>       # give it back
showrunner role roster               # every seat, its state, and its holder's liveness basis
```

`enter` never blocks — a SessionStart hook cannot — so it is where the *prompt* lives. `guard` is
where the *enforcement* lives, and it denies on exactly one condition: the lease is HELD by a
**different live session**. FREE, STALE and UNREADABLE all allow, and none of the three is an
oversight — a stale holder is proved dead, and an unreadable one cannot be adjudicated at all, so
refusing on it would wedge a tree on somebody's partial write.

**The guard is exactly as present as its registration.** It runs from a tracked shim,
`.showrunner/hooks/worktree-guard.sh`, registered as a PreToolUse hook. `git worktree add`
copies tracked files only, and a hook that does not cross into a worktree cannot guard one — so
the shim needs one of two arrangements, and `doctor` names which one you are in:

* **tracked** — commit it and git carries it. The simplest thing when a repo allows it.
* **ignored** — `spawn` provisions it into each worktree instead. This is the arrangement for a
  shared repo that keeps `.showrunner/` out of its history (`.git/info/exclude`), where "commit
  it" is the one action you cannot take.

**Neither is the only state with no answer**, and it warns: git will not carry the file, and
provisioning refuses to, because copying it would hand the Crawler something its own `git add -A`
commits onto its branch — which then collides with the same untracked path in the main checkout.

`showrunner doctor` reports the shim, its arrangement and its registration separately, because a
guard nobody registered has never once run.

**It fails OPEN and says so.** No binary, no payload, an exception — all allow, and all print
that the call was allowed without being checked. A PreToolUse that hard-fails on its own plumbing
blocks every write including the one that would repair it.

There is still no `lease take` verb: a lease is acquired by `enter` and `fork`, and
`lease status` is how you read the result. A lease is released when its tree is removed, and a
wedged one is cleared by name — `showrunner lock release worktree:<tree> --force`, which is the
remedy the UNREADABLE refusal prints.

**A second hook, on Stop.** `.showrunner/hooks/inert-crawler-gate.sh` refuses the ORCHESTRATOR's
turn-end while `waiting` reports a Crawler that is alive and inert — refused at its own turn-end,
needing a message rather than time. `waiting` already knew; nothing consulted it at the one moment
that decides anything, and a run stalled until a human noticed. It fails open on every unknown, it
offers `reap` beside messaging (a block can mean gone rather than waiting), and it does not fire
inside a Crawler's own worktree — a Crawler cannot message or reap its siblings.

Read `waiting --porcelain`, not the prose, if you build anything on this. The BLOCKED lines are
printed on stdout AND stderr now, and BLOCKED has its own exit code — but a verb whose finding,
verdict and status live on three channels will be integrated against incorrectly, and the idiom
`waiting || exit 0` still swallows the blocked case because it collapses every non-zero code. The
JSON is the contract; the prose is for a person.

A worktree had an owner on paper (`campaign.json`) and no holder in fact — nothing consulted that
record when a second session opened the directory and started editing. A lease's holder is a live
process. `pid_basis` says how that pid was learned, because a hook is handed no PID and the
answer comes from walking an ancestry, which can land on a weaker fact. Read it: a lease resting
on `ppid-fallback` is worth less than one resting on `ancestor-claude`.

It does **not** stop a human in an editor, a shell script or a `git checkout` — only Claude Code
sessions consult it. And it protects the *tree*: two sessions in different trees still share the
git common dir, the lock root, the graph and the campaign record.

**A BLOCKED Crawler needs a message, not time.** It was refused at its turn-end, it is alive, and
nothing here can prompt it — `reap` correctly proposes nothing and every other signal reads
healthy. Send it something in its room. If chat is disabled you have no way to reach it, which is
why the room is not optional under `--launch`.

**Do not fan out past what `plan` allows.** Two leaves can be mutually unblocked and still be the same
edit: the graph models dependencies, not files. A false collision costs one wave of latency; a missed
one costs a merge conflict in an unattended run with nobody watching.

**`--finding` is worth using.** Where you have already checked a premise, put your finding *and its
evidence* in the brief and ask the Crawler to confirm or refute it rather than to trust it. An
independent confirmation with line numbers is worth strictly more than either reading alone.

**On resume, reconcile before doing anything.** An abandoned worktree may hold the only copy of real
work: surface it, do not silently reuse it and do not silently delete it.

## Several CAMPAIGNS in one checkout

A campaign is smaller than a repo. The natural unit of a body of work is often a story, and the
handoff a showrunner charges — worktrees, briefs, rooms, integration — is only paid for by the
parallelism it buys. So more than one at a time in one checkout is the ORDINARY case.

```
SHOWRUNNER_CAMPAIGN=my-campaign showrunner status    # state nests under a per-campaign directory
```

Graph, campaign record, event journal and scratch all follow the campaign. **Locks deliberately do
not.** A lock names a physical single-consumer resource — a device, a bound port — shared by the
machine and not by a body of work, so two campaigns flashing the same TV must serialize against
each other. Per-campaign lock roots would give each its own and let both hold it at once: a mutex
that is quietly a no-op.

With no campaign selected every path resolves exactly as it always did, so an existing checkout is
untouched. An env var rather than a flag because a flag has to be threaded through every verb, and
any verb that forgot it would silently answer about a different campaign.

The worktree root stays repo-wide, so two campaigns naming the same leaf collide on a path — a loud
refusal, not a clobber. The project name still defaults to the repo's own, so campaigns in one
checkout share a chat prefix unless you set one.

## Roles: showrunner checks the shape, never the meaning

Names and meaning are yours, the way lane rules already are. showrunner knows only two things: how
a seat is obtained, and what the fields a guard reads say. Definitions live at a user-level path
(`roles.json` under your config home) because an in-repo config is writable by the very session it
constrains — measured, not assumed. A project may ADD a role there, never redefine one.

Two acquisition modes are the whole model, and they replace any lead/worker taxonomy, because that
distinction was never about names — it was about how the seat is obtained:

| | |
|---|---|
| `claim` | a session TAKES an open seat. Exclusive, first-come, with pid+boot liveness so a dead holder's seat is reclaimable. The only way a from-scratch session can get one. |
| `assign` | written by whoever CREATED the session, before it existed. A session holding one cannot claim. The campaign record IS that writing: `spawn` names the tree's leaf before the session exists, keyed to its worktree, and `seat_roles` is what reads it back. |

`seat_roles` maps a **derived seat** onto one of your roles. Without it `assign` had no reader, so
every Crawler resolved to the fallback and ran under the fallback's policy *inside the worktree
`spawn` had just made for it* — with a deny-everything fallback, an audit leaf finished only by
routing its evidence around the write guard with shell redirection. A guard whose reward for
holding is a workaround teaches every later session to route around it.

```json
{"roles": {"...": {}}, "seat_roles": {"crawler": "worker"}}
```

Same authority as the definitions: **user level wins**, and a project may map a seat the user left
unmapped but never remap one — a project that could remap its own seat would hand itself any role
in the catalog, which is the widening the definitions left the repo to prevent. A conflict is
reported, not resolved silently.

Two halves keep this record-based rather than location-based. Only a worktree the campaign record
NAMES resolves, so `git worktree add` is not a way to grant yourself a role. And **`orchestrator`
ships unmapped on purpose** — standing in the main checkout is a location, not a record, and
authority by location is the failure this whole seam replaced. Map it yourself if you want it.

Fields showrunner checks: `acquire`, `capacity`, `reports_to`, `may_create`, `writes`. `notes` is
your prose and is announced as explicitly unchecked. `doctor` refuses a dangling `reports_to` or
`may_create`, a `reports_to` cycle, an org with no root, nothing claimable at all, a fallback
role that may create something — which would make the fallback a way around the policy — and a
`seat_roles` entry pointing at a role nothing defines, because that seat resolves to the fallback
and one typo would otherwise buy the whole write denial back, silently.

**With no roles defined, no dispatch policy is enforced for anybody.** That is deliberate:
inventing one would refuse the dispatches of every consumer who never wrote any.

### Getting a seat, and keeping it

Both modes had to become reachable before either worked. `assign` had no reader until a seat could
resolve through `seat_roles`; `claim` had no writer at all — `roles.claim` was a library function
nothing called, and the `claim` VERB claims a leaf. So on a stock install every session resolved
to the fallback whatever its roles said.

```
showrunner role claim campaign-lead --who agent-a
showrunner role roster
showrunner role release campaign-lead
```

`role claim` refuses a role declaring `acquire: "assign"`: its whole meaning is that whoever
created the session decided, so taking it here would be self-nomination into a seat the model says
cannot be self-nominated. That one is obtained by `seat_roles`.

**A CLAIM'S PID IS DISCOVERED, NOT HANDED OVER**, and this is the difference between a seat and a
seat-shaped file. Liveness is a pid plus a boot token, so a claim keyed to the short-lived process
that *made* the call is dead the moment that call returns: it reports success, the roster reads
STALE, the resolver skips it, and `whoami` announces the fallback again. Reported from a real
seating attempt and recovered only by walking the process ancestry by hand — which `util.session_pid`
already did, with a `basis` separating "proved it" from "could not tell". `lock acquire` prints the
same warning for the same reason; the roles path shared its mechanism and not its mitigation. A pid
that cannot be resolved is REFUSED rather than recorded, following `lease`: a claim with no
liveness is not a weaker claim, it is a lock nothing can ever reclaim.

`role roster` exists because that state had nowhere to be seen. The only way to notice a dead
claim was calling `roles.roster()` from Python, and a state nothing surfaces is a state nobody
debugs.

### A guard cannot consume prose

`whoami` emitted prose and nothing else, so a hook author who needed the resolved role had no way
to ask for it. A consumer's `PreToolUse` write guard therefore carried its own copy of the
resolver; when a seat learned to resolve through `seat_roles` the copy did not, so the
announcement said one role while the guard enforced the deny-everything fallback and a session was
correctly unable to edit the file it had been dispatched to edit. Two statements of one policy,
free to disagree — the failure `enforced_lines` prevents *inside* the announcement, arriving from
outside it.

```
showrunner whoami --porcelain
```

emits the seat, the evidence, the resolved role and how it was resolved, and the
`writes`/`may_create`/`reports_to`/`acquire` a guard actually enforces. `whoami` RENDERS this same
dict, so the prose and the JSON cannot drift. Branch on **`enforced`**: it is false whenever
showrunner enforces nothing, and a null `role` must never be read as "no restriction" — that is
the fail-open reading, and `problems` says which case it is. The porcelain exits non-zero if it
could not resolve at all, so a parser can fail closed; the prose path still exits 0, because a
SessionStart hook cannot block.

## The two seams showrunner did not own, and now does

```
showrunner whoami                    # SessionStart AND PostCompact  (whoami.sh)
showrunner dispatch guard            # PreToolUse on BASH            (dispatch-guard.sh)
```

Both run from tracked shims under `.showrunner/hooks/`, beside `worktree-guard.sh`,
`inert-crawler-gate.sh` and `waiting-probe.sh`. `worktree register` wires all of them; a guard
nobody registers has never once run, which was true of one of these between building it and
noticing.

`whoami` announces what this session IS. The seat is **derived** — a linked worktree is a CRAWLER
and the campaign record names its leaf; the main checkout of a repo carrying a campaign is the
ORCHESTRATOR; no campaign is SOLO, said out loud rather than left to look like an idle
orchestrator; and UNKNOWN is a real answer, announced as one. There is no file a session can write
to become something else.

On **both** seams, because a rule that survives only until the next compaction is a rule for the
first hour. The announcement carries the load-bearing lines rather than pointing at a file to
read, and its ENFORCED block is generated from the role fields the guards actually read — prose in
one place and enforcement in another is two statements of one policy, free to disagree.

`dispatch guard` refuses a raw headless `claude` dispatch from a session whose role may not create
one. On BASH, which is the mechanism actually used: a version of this matched on `Agent` guarded
the in-process subagent tool while 42 consecutive real dispatches went out through Bash, reporting
nothing. It cannot see a command built from a shell variable, a wrapper script, or any non-Bash
tool — the LEASE is what protects a tree from whatever gets in anyway.

## When a run could not measure anything

```
showrunner check     # exit 0 no new failures · 2 new failures · 3 VOID · 1 no baseline
```

A run that could not reach the world did not measure anything, and its failure count carries no
information. That is strictly worse than a degraded comparison, because a degraded comparison is
still about the code. `check` screens for unreachable-world signatures — DNS failure, connection
refused, no route to host — ahead of the comparison and exits **3**, distinct from 2, so a caller
treating non-zero as "the code is bad" gets a code it did not map rather than a wrong answer it
will believe. Add your own with `void_patterns`; a pattern that will not compile is reported as
UNSCREENED rather than skipped.

VALID means "no evidence the world was unreachable" — never "the environment was sound". A partial
outage that resolved mid-run, a backend serving wrong data, or a device degrading without a network
error all read as VALID, and the verdict says so.

### A blocked report is a fact about the past

`waiting` no longer reports a Crawler as BLOCKED when its **tree disagrees**. A commit on its
branch, or a tracked file in its own worktree changed since the block was recorded, means it is
working without a channel to report on — legitimate waiting, and it is counted as live.

This exists because a chat outage produced the opposite: a Crawler went inert (its only
reporting channel was gone), the gate refused the ORCHESTRATOR's turn-end, and both remedies it
offered were unavailable or destructive — message it, which needed the dead bus, or reap it,
which releases the claim and surfaces a tree holding live uncommitted work. After an
out-of-band wake it kept refusing while the Crawler was demonstrably working, because "inert"
was inferred from the room and never from the tree.

**Tree evidence only ever RELEASES.** No recorded block, an unreadable tree, a missing branch or
a disagreeing clock all yield no evidence, which is exactly today's behaviour. Only TRACKED
files count: a log the harness writes or an editor swapfile would otherwise release a gate with
nobody having done any work, and a false positive is the expensive direction for a signal whose
job is to stop refusing.

## If several orchestrators are running at once

Supported. Do NOT read `ready` and claim its first entry — everyone gets the same list:

```
showrunner claim --next --actor <you>    # atomically take any free leaf; exit 1 when dry
showrunner waiting                       # exit 0 waiting · 1 not waiting · 3 a Crawler is BLOCKED
                                         # A Crawler refused at a turn-end is live and counts as
                                         # NEITHER waiting nor parked — only a message restarts
                                         # it. 3 is its own code so a caller treating non-zero as
                                         # "no" cannot miss the one case it exists for. Build on
                                         # --porcelain: the finding is on BOTH streams now, but
                                         # three exit codes and two streams combine wrongly.
```

Losing a claim race is not an error; a sibling got there first. Integration and single-consumer
resources stay exclusive and **refuse** rather than queue, so a refusal there means "someone else
is mid-merge", not "something broke".

## If you are a CRAWLER

Your brief is in your scratch dir (`BRIEF.md`). The short version:

**1. Verify the premise before you write anything.** The issue was written from an incident, and the
incident may have happened in a different repo, a different harness, or a version of this code that no
longer exists. Three of fourteen issues in one real run described something that was not true here;
in a later batch of seven, all seven held. The rate is not the point — you cannot tell which batch
you are in from the inside, and the two look identical until you read the source.

**2b. "Unreachable" is a THIRD outcome.** A true premise attached to code nothing reaches is
void, and the premise check cannot catch it — that asks *is this true of the code*, this asks
*does anything get here*, and the answer is in files the brief never named. Observed twice in
one hour: a genuinely malformed colour matrix on a preset an allowlist dropped five months
earlier, and a real branch defect gated on `count <= 4` where the only client sends 40.

```
showrunner close <leaf> --unreachable --evidence <allowlist|caller|enumeration> \
    --premise holds --reason "<what nothing reaches, and how you know>"
```

`done` claims a user-visible change that does not exist; `refuted` says the analysis was wrong
when it was right. A Crawler forced to choose picks `done`, because by then it holds a real
commit and real tests. Where a UI is involved, WALK THE UI — a picker is enumerated somewhere
the source read will not show you.

**2. "Premise refuted" is a success.** Close it and stop; do not build a smaller version of the thing
so you have something to show:

```
showrunner close <leaf> --refuted --evidence <file> --reason "<what is actually true>"
```

**3. Close through the gate.** It refuses unless you name a real, non-empty artifact that is *newer
than your claim*, and unless you state the premise verdict with the file you checked it against:

```
showrunner close <leaf> --proof <path> --premise holds|partial|refuted|unverifiable \
    --premise-read <path> --reason "<what you did>"
```

A RELATIVE PATH IS RESOLVED AGAINST THE TREE YOU ARE STANDING IN, so the artifact you just wrote
in your own worktree is the one read. It used to be joined against the main checkout, which found
that checkout's stale copy of the same relative path and refused the close as proof older than the
claim — the one verdict the gate exists to produce, manufactured from a correct submission, and
invisible to anyone who happened to pass absolute paths. A cwd outside this repo's trees falls back
to the main checkout, and a refusal now names the tree it read from.

**4. Write non-repo files in YOUR OWN scratch dir**, the one named in your brief. Commit messages,
captured output, fixtures, before/after artifacts. Not a shared temp dir. In a real run two Crawlers
independently picked the same obvious filename and one nearly committed the other's commit message
onto its own changes — a real commit, plausible message, describing work it does not contain, every
gate green. You and your siblings are the same model solving similar tasks from similar prompts, so
you converge on the same obvious filename far more often than independent actors would.

**5. Run single-consumer commands through the lock**, never directly:

```
showrunner lock run <resource> --holder <you> -- <command>
```

The lock is a guarantee only where the *consumer* takes it. `lock guard` catches the honest mistake; a
raw command that matches no pattern escapes it.

**6. If a shared-state gate refuses you, wait or escalate. Never bypass.** Your worktree isolates
tracked files and nothing else — the harness's state directory, lock paths and caches are shared, so a
gate may be reporting on a tree you do not own. `--no-verify` starts looking reasonable exactly when
you are stuck under a mandate to finish, and that is the moment it is most wrong.

**7. If your turn-end is refused, your leaf is still open — close it or say why.** That refusal is
showrunner's own gate reading the graph, and it is telling you the truth. Do not treat it as a
signal to stop: a headless session that stops there has nothing that can restart it from inside,
and the orchestrator sees a live process on an open leaf with every artifact looking finished.
One sat 44 minutes that way.

**8. In your room, post what the orchestrator can ACT on — and no start notice.** It dispatched you
seconds ago and wrote your brief; it has that content already. A refuted premise, a collision with
another leaf, a blocker, a decision you cannot make alone, your verdict at close. Under a turn-end
gate an announcement is indistinguishable from a question, so a wave of N Crawlers saying hello
costs N blocked turn-ends on the one party whose attention is not parallel.

## Usage limits

A Crawler parked at a usage limit is **not dead** and its claim must survive:

```
showrunner park <leaf> --reason "usage limit — window resets at <time>"
showrunner unpark <leaf>
```

A parked leaf is excluded from `reap` and does not block `stop-gate`, but it is still reported.

## The gates, as hooks

Both exit **2**, which is the Claude Code PreToolUse deny code:

```
showrunner lock guard -- <the proposed command>   # blocks a single-consumer verb while held
showrunner stop-gate [--leaf <id>] [--tree <path>] # refuses a turn-end while YOUR leaf is open
```

`stop-gate` excludes epics (a container is expected to sit in progress while its children are worked)
and parked leaves (accounted-for work, not abandoned work).

**`spawn --launch` wires `stop-gate --leaf <id>` into the Crawler's own tree** — merged into the
harness's turn-end triggers, never replacing what is already there, and with no timeout of its
own so the harness's budget governs. You do not wire it by hand.

**The `--leaf` is load-bearing.** Without it the gate asks "is *any* leaf open in this campaign",
and since the same gate is written into every Crawler's triggers, each one is gated on all of its
siblings: with N dispatched, N−1 are structurally guaranteed to be refused at least once, the
refusal advises them to close work in worktrees they cannot reach, and a headless Crawler has no
next turn in which to act on it. Given no `--leaf`, the gate falls back to matching the caller's
worktree against `claim_tree`, which is why a manual `claim` records the tree it was made from.

Both of those defects came from wiring this gate at all: this section once described both gates as
hooks with no path into a Crawler, which made the stop gate real, documented and unreachable.
Reaching it produced the BLOCKED state above, and reaching it *unscoped* produced this.

## Checks: no NEW failures, never "all green"

```
showrunner baseline    # on a known-good tree
showrunner check       # compare; exit 2 on a NEW failure
```

A repo with pre-existing failures cannot satisfy "all green", so that version of the gate gets
switched off on contact with a real codebase. If a check fails without producing parseable failure
lines, the comparison degrades to exit-code granularity and **says so** — reduced resolution must
never read as a clean comparison.

## Integration commits

```
showrunner integration-commit --crawler <name> [--crawler <name> ...]
```

A provenance check keyed to "did *you* edit this?" answers no for every integration commit, correctly:
Crawlers wrote the files, `git merge` brought them in. The useful question is different — *does the
staged set match the union of what the merged Crawlers edited?* — and it catches the real failure: a
file in an integration commit that **no Crawler ever touched**.

## The work graph

```
showrunner add "<title>" [--id X] [--body-file F] [--label L] [--after <blocking-leaf>]
showrunner dep <child> <parent>      # child is blocked by parent
showrunner edit <leaf> [--title T] [--body-file F] [--paths P]
showrunner list|show|ready|claim|release|park|unpark
```

**`edit` exists because the body IS the brief.** A leaf's body is interpolated into the document a
Crawler works from, so a wrong one dispatches a wrong task — and before this verb there was no way
back: `add` refuses an existing id, and the only exit was to close the leaf, which spends the
proof-of-done gate on a decision that never happened. It refuses on a leaf that is not open, so it
cannot rewrite the instructions under a Crawler already working from them. Fix the body *before*
you spawn.

Backend is `auto`: an existing `br` graph is used when present, otherwise a vendored `sqlite3` graph.
Everything else in showrunner talks to one interface and never learns which it got. Note that `br`
records no liveness on a claim, so `reap` cannot work against it and says so rather than reporting
"nothing is stale".

## Which code am I running?

```
showrunner --version
```

Answers with a **commit**, not just `0.1.0` — and resolves it from where the CODE lives, never
from the cwd. Under a central install the cwd is some consumer project, so answering from it
would report that project's HEAD as showrunner's version. Three provenances, and only two of
them can name a commit:

| | what names it |
|---|---|
| **pinned** | `self --pin` extracted it from a git ref; `VERSION`/`PINNED` sit beside the code. The strongest answer, and why central mode can say what every project on the machine runs. |
| **checkout** | the code lives in a showrunner git repo — its root IS the repo root. Reports HEAD, and whether the tree is dirty, because uncommitted edits make that sha an overstatement. |
| **copy** | `install.sh` without `--central` copies from a working tree. **No commit names this code**, and none is invented — that absence is the argument for pinning. |

`__version__` alone was `0.1.0` for the project's whole life and never bumped, so it could not
distinguish a checkout from this morning from an install three weeks stale.

## One copy of the code, every project's own config

Per-project install is the **default** and stays the documented path. Central is opt-in, one
flag, and reversible in both directions:

```
./install.sh --central /path/to/project      # write ONE dispatcher shim, no local copy of the code
showrunner self --pin <ref> --dest <path>    # populate central: extract bin/ and lib/ at a git ref
                                             # RUN FROM A SHOWRUNNER CHECKOUT: the ref is resolved
                                             # in the repo the RUNNING CODE lives in, never in the
                                             # project you are standing in. From a consumer repo it
                                             # refuses rather than publishing their HEAD as the tool.
showrunner self --dest <path>                # what is pinned there; exit 2 if it was edited since
./install.sh /path/to/project                # revert: restore the local copy, drop the dependency
```

Under `--central`, `.showrunner/bin/showrunner` stops being the tool and becomes ~20 lines of
bash that exec a shared copy at `$SHOWRUNNER_CENTRAL` (default `~/.claude/showrunner-central`).
The shim is machine-agnostic and byte-identical in every project, so a consumer who commits it
anyway is not committing anything about their machine.

**Only the CODE is shared.** There is no `SHOWRUNNER_HOME` equivalent and none is needed:
`config.load` resolves the project from the cwd's git root, so the central binary run inside a
consumer repo — or inside one of its worktrees — reads THAT repo's config, graph and locks.

**When central is missing, the fail posture splits.** Hook verbs (`lock guard`,
`worktree guard`, `worktree enter`, `stop-gate`) exit 0, because a PreToolUse that hard-fails on
its own plumbing blocks the write that would repair it — **and they say `ALLOWED WITHOUT BEING
CHECKED`**, because an allow nobody is told about is indistinguishable from a guard that ran and
was content. Every other verb exits 1 naming the populate command.

`lock run` is deliberately **not** a hook verb. Routing and guarding are optimisations; `lock
run` is the guarantee, and it still fails loud. A missing central install costs the optimisation
and keeps the guarantee — which is the whole reason this fail posture is acceptable.

**This does not make showrunner a global command.** The entrypoint is still
`./.showrunner/bin/showrunner`; central changes what that file *is*, not where you type it. And
`VERSION` names what was *extracted* — nothing hashes the central directory afterwards, so one
bad pin still reaches every project on the machine at once.

Pinned to a **named ref**, never copied from a working tree, so "what is central running" answers
with a commit that can be checked out and diffed. `VERSION` holds the resolved SHA and `PINNED`
holds the ref, SHA and time; if the two ever disagree, something edited the directory after the
pin and `self --dest` refuses rather than picking one.

It will only ever overwrite a destination it recognises as its own pin — a mistyped `--dest` is
refused, not emptied. What it does **not** establish: `VERSION` names what was *extracted*, not
what is there now. Nothing hashes the contents.

## Verifying the tool itself

```
python3 test/run.py        # 1005 assertions; needs only Python 3 + git
bash prototype/demo.sh     # the original shell POC: 7 run anywhere, 5 skip loudly
```

Assertions needing `br` or `tmux` skip loudly, naming the dependency. Nothing here asks you to take a
passing suite on trust.

## Deeper docs

- `README.md` — the human-facing overview.
- `docs/DESIGN.md` — the decisions, the failure modes, and what is still open.
- `lib/showrunner/` — the implementation; every module's docstring says which failure it exists to
  prevent.
